title: Avuha bar Ihi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was a great man in Shmuel’s time. In Nazir 24b, Shmuel told him, “Do not sit down until you explain this teaching to me.” In Bava Metzia 14a, Avuha bar Ihi bought an upper room from his sister, and a creditor seized it from him. He came before Mar Shmuel, who asked, “Did she give you a warranty?” “No.” “If so, go in peace.” He replied, “But is it not the Master who said—”, etc. In Bava Metzia 75a, Shmuel told him, “Lend me a hundred peppercorns for a hundred and twenty, and it is proper.” In Eruvin 74a: that [alley] in which Ivut bar Ihi lived (Hyman says it should read Avuha, following Dikdukei Soferim)—he made a lechi, a side-post for its entrance, and Mar Shmuel permitted it. Rav Anan came after Shmuel’s death and threw it down, etc. He and his brother Minyamin were very pious. In Megillah 28a, Avuha bar Ihi and Minyamin bar Ihi: one said, “May I be rewarded, for I never gazed at a Cuthean”; the other said, “May I be rewarded, for I never entered into a partnership with a Cuthean.” Ketubot 61a relates that one gave his attendant some of every dish, while the other gave him only one kind; Elijah conversed with one, but did not converse with the other.

notes.text: Bava Metzia14a has Avuha buying from his sister, not selling her room; the response is “go in peace.” Arikh in the peppercorn example means fitting/proper, not long. Shamash in Ketubot61a is an attendant who is fed. The brothers’ contrasting practices and Elijah’s response are preserved without deciding which brother followed which practice.

Bava Metzia 14a directly has Avuha buying from his sister and being told to go in peace; 75a directly gives the peppercorn exchange. The alley episode runs from Eruvin 74a into 74b, reading Ayvut bar Ihi; it also gives an alternative food-versus-lodging explanation after the lechi is removed. The precise Dikdukei Soferim Avuha correction and the post-Shmuel-death chronology remain Hyman’s. Ketubot 61a leaves the two brothers’ feeding practices and Elijah’s contrasting responses assigned only to one and the other.
